framework.name: College Board AP Course Frameworks
framework.source: https://apcentral.collegeboard.org (AP Course and Exam Descriptions; unit names follow the frameworks, objective wording is the school's own)

objectives.description: Identify the exigence, audience, purpose and speaker in a text, and explain how they shape it.
Explain how a writer's claim and line of reasoning respond to a rhetorical situation.
Describe how the parts of a text, such as introduction, evidence and conclusion, serve the writer's purpose.
Write a thesis that takes a defensible position on a rhetorical analysis prompt.
Distinguish a claim from the evidence offered for it, and judge whether the evidence is relevant and sufficient.
Analyze how a writer uses ethos, pathos and logos in a speech or essay.
Write a body paragraph that links a piece of evidence to the claim with commentary.
Explain how a writer uses anecdote, statistics and authority to support a claim.
Analyze how a writer's organization, such as chronological, spatial or comparative, supports the argument.
Explain how transitions and the order of ideas guide the reader through a line of reasoning.
Write a rhetorical analysis essay with a thesis, evidence and commentary that explains the writer's choices.
Read several sources on one issue and identify points of agreement and disagreement.
Integrate evidence from sources into your own argument using paraphrase, summary and quotation.
Cite sources accurately in a standard format and avoid plagiarism.
Analyze how diction, syntax and figurative language contribute to a writer's tone.
Revise sentences for variety, concision and emphasis, and explain the effect of each change.
Write a timed argument essay that defends a position using evidence from your reading and experience.
Reflect on feedback from a scoring rubric and set a goal for the next essay.
Describe a character's traits, motives and changes as a short story develops.
Explain how setting shapes mood, character and conflict in a story.
Analyze how a narrator's point of view affects what the reader learns and how they judge it.
Write a thesis about how an author's choices create meaning in a short story.
Analyze how imagery and figurative language build meaning in a poem.
Explain how form, structure and line breaks contribute to the poem's effect.
Describe how a speaker's tone shifts across a poem and what the shift reveals.
Compare how two poems treat a similar subject.
Trace how a theme develops across a novel or a play from beginning to end.
Analyze how the structure of a longer work, such as its sequence and its subplots, shapes its meaning.
Explain how a symbol or motif recurs and deepens across a long work.
Analyze the relationship between two characters and what it shows about the work's central conflict.
Write a literary argument that defends an interpretation with evidence and commentary.
Use quotations and paraphrase accurately and explain how each supports the claim.
Revise a thesis so it is specific, defensible and about the work's meaning.
Write a timed essay on a poem and a timed essay on a prose passage.
Lead a discussion of a text by asking questions that invite interpretation.
Reflect on your growth as a reader and writer using feedback from a scoring rubric.
Explain the ideas of natural rights, popular sovereignty and social contract in the Declaration of Independence.
Compare the Federalist No. 10 and Brutus No. 1 arguments about the size of a republic.
Describe how the Constitution's design provides separation of powers and checks and balances.
Explain how the debate over federalism has shaped the relationship of the states and the national government.
Compare the Articles of Confederation with the Constitution and explain why the framers replaced them.
Explain how the Constitution's ratification and its amendments reflect compromise.
Describe the structure, powers and leadership of Congress, including the House and the Senate.
Explain how Congress uses its powers of oversight, the budget and committees.
Describe the formal and informal powers of the president and the role of the bureaucracy.
Explain how the Supreme Court uses judicial review and how its decisions are limited.
Analyze how the branches interact in making and carrying out policy.

strands.strand: Unit 3: Civil Liberties and Civil Rights
strands.subStrand: Unit 3: Civil Liberties and Civil Rights

objectives.description: Explain how the Bill of Rights has been incorporated against the states.
Apply the First Amendment cases required for the course to a new scenario.
Describe how civil rights movements used the courts, protest and legislation to expand equality.
Read and interpret a required foundational document, such as Federalist No. 10, and explain its argument.
Analyze quantitative data in a chart or a table about political behavior.
Write a short argument essay that makes a claim and supports it with evidence from a foundational document.
Apply a landmark Supreme Court case to a new situation and explain the reasoning.
Explain scarcity, opportunity cost and comparative advantage using a production possibilities curve.
Calculate absolute and comparative advantage and the terms of trade.
Explain how supply and demand determine market equilibrium and what shifts them.
Analyze the effect of a price ceiling or floor on a market, with a graph.

strands.strand: Unit 2: Economic Indicators and the Business Cycle
strands.subStrand: Unit 2: Economic Indicators and the Business Cycle

objectives.description: Calculate and interpret GDP by the expenditure approach and distinguish nominal from real GDP.
Calculate the unemployment rate and describe types of unemployment.
Measure inflation with the consumer price index and explain how it affects people differently.
Describe the phases of the business cycle and their effects on output and employment.

strands.strand: Unit 3: National Income and Price Determination
strands.subStrand: Unit 3: National Income and Price Determination

objectives.description: Explain aggregate demand and aggregate supply and what shifts them.
Use the AD-AS model to show the short-run effects of a shock.
Explain the multiplier and calculate its effect on spending.
Describe how the economy returns to long-run equilibrium.
Explain the functions of money and measures of the money supply.
Describe how banks create money and how the money multiplier works.
Analyze the money market and the loanable funds market with graphs.
Draw and label a graph that illustrates an economic change and explain the result in words.
Interpret recent government data from FRED and explain what it shows about the economy.
Write a free-response answer that defines, graphs and explains the effect of a policy.
Describe the major perspectives in psychology and the questions each asks.
Compare descriptive, correlational and experimental methods and say what each can show.
Design a simple experiment and identify the independent variable, dependent variable and controls.
Explain why research must follow ethical guidelines and name the safeguards that exist.
Read a graph or a correlation and avoid concluding causation without an experiment.
Describe the structure of a neuron and how neurons communicate.
Explain the roles of neurotransmitters in mood, movement and memory.
Name the major structures of the brain and the functions of each lobe.
Describe how the endocrine system and the nervous system work together.
Explain how nature and nurture interact, using twin and adoption studies.
Describe how sensory receptors turn physical energy into neural signals.
Compare bottom-up and top-down processing in perception.
Explain depth perception and perceptual constancies.
Compare classical and operant conditioning and give an example of each.
Apply schedules of reinforcement and explain how they shape behavior.
Describe observational learning and Bandura's Bobo doll study.
Write a response that defines a term and applies it to a scenario.
Interpret a data table from a study and state a conclusion.
Explain how the structure and properties of water support life.
Describe the structure and function of carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.
Explain how a protein's levels of structure determine its function.
Describe the structure of DNA and RNA and how they differ.
Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and describe the functions of the organelles.
Explain how surface area to volume ratio limits cell size.
Describe the fluid mosaic model and the movement of substances across a membrane.
Predict the movement of water using water potential.
Explain how compartmentalization increases the efficiency of a cell.
Explain how enzymes lower activation energy, and how inhibitors and conditions change their rate.
Describe the light-dependent and light-independent reactions of photosynthesis.
Describe the stages of cellular respiration and where ATP is made.
Compare aerobic respiration and fermentation.

strands.strand: Unit 4: Cell Communication and Cell Cycle
strands.subStrand: Unit 4: Cell Communication and Cell Cycle

objectives.description: Describe the stages of cell signaling and give an example of a pathway.
Explain how feedback regulates a biological process.
Describe the cell cycle and how checkpoints control it.
Analyze data from an experiment with a control and justify a claim from the results.
Perform a statistical test, such as chi-square, and say what the result means.
Describe the flow of energy through food chains and food webs and the loss at each level.
Explain the carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and water cycles and how humans change them.
Describe how terrestrial and aquatic biomes differ and what limits productivity in each.
Explain the role of primary production and its measure in an ecosystem.
Describe the three levels of biodiversity and why each matters.
Explain how ecosystem services benefit people.
Describe the causes of habitat loss and the effects of invasive species.
Explain ecological succession and how a disturbance changes a community.
Calculate population growth rate and doubling time.
Compare exponential and logistic growth and explain carrying capacity.
Distinguish r-selected and K-selected species and age structure diagrams.
Explain how human population growth is affected by fertility, mortality and development.
Describe the layers of the Earth and plate tectonics.
Explain how soils form and how soil properties affect agriculture.
Describe atmospheric layers and the causes of global wind patterns.
Explain how weather, climate and El Nino affect ecosystems.
Design an investigation of a local environmental question and analyze the data.
Evaluate the costs and benefits of a solution to an environmental problem.
Estimate a limit from a graph and a table and describe what it means.
Evaluate limits algebraically using factoring, rationalizing and the properties of limits.
Determine whether a function is continuous at a point and classify discontinuities.
Use limits to describe infinite limits and end behavior.
State and apply the Intermediate Value Theorem.

strands.strand: Unit 2: Differentiation: Definition and Fundamental Properties
strands.subStrand: Unit 2: Differentiation: Definition and Fundamental Properties

objectives.description: Define the derivative as a limit of the difference quotient and interpret it as an instantaneous rate.
Find the equation of a tangent line to a curve at a point.
Use the power, product and quotient rules to find derivatives.
Differentiate sine, cosine, exponential and logarithmic functions.
Describe the relationship between differentiability and continuity.

strands.strand: Unit 3: Differentiation: Composite, Implicit and Inverse Functions
strands.subStrand: Unit 3: Differentiation: Composite, Implicit and Inverse Functions

objectives.description: Differentiate composite functions using the chain rule.
Differentiate implicitly and find a tangent line to an implicit curve.
Find the derivative of an inverse function.
Differentiate inverse trigonometric functions.
Interpret the derivative as a rate of change in a real context, with units.
Solve a related-rates problem.
Justify a conclusion with a theorem, naming its conditions.
Communicate a solution with correct notation and units.
Distinguish categorical from quantitative variables and display each appropriately.
Describe a distribution by its shape, center, spread and outliers.
Compute and interpret the mean, median, standard deviation and interquartile range.
Use the empirical rule and z-scores to compare values from different distributions.
Compare two or more distributions using side-by-side graphs and summary statistics.
Describe an association in a scatterplot by form, direction and strength.
Calculate and interpret the correlation coefficient and its limits.
Fit a least-squares regression line and interpret the slope and intercept in context.
Use residual plots to judge whether a linear model is appropriate.
Explain why association does not imply causation, and recognize lurking variables.
Distinguish an observational study from an experiment.
Describe a simple random sample, a stratified sample and a cluster sample.
Identify sources of bias in a survey.
Design an experiment with random assignment, a control and blinding.

strands.strand: Unit 4: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
strands.subStrand: Unit 4: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions

objectives.description: Use the rules of probability, including the addition and multiplication rules.
Calculate conditional probability and decide whether two events are independent.
Write a conclusion that interprets a result in context and states the reasoning.
Use technology to compute statistics and explain the output.
Declare and initialize variables of primitive and reference types.
Evaluate expressions with arithmetic operators, integer division and casting.
Call methods on objects, including String methods, and use the Math class.
Create objects with constructors and describe the parts of a class.
Write conditional statements using boolean expressions and relational operators.
Combine conditions with and, or and not, and apply De Morgan's laws.
Write while and for loops and trace their output.
Use nested loops to produce patterns and process data.
Develop and trace algorithms that use loops and conditions.
Write a class with private instance variables, constructors and accessor and mutator methods.
Explain the scope of variables and the meaning of the this keyword.
Write static methods and variables and say when to use them.
Document a class with comments and preconditions and postconditions.
Create and traverse a one-dimensional array.
Use an ArrayList to add, remove and search for elements.
Write algorithms for searching and sorting.
Debug a program by reading error messages and tracing values.
Discuss the ethical and social impacts of a computing innovation.
